passages.t: The man in linen and the mark
passages.happening:
God calls the executioners of the city. Six men come from the Upper Gate, each with a weapon, and with them ‘another man clothed in linen who had a writing kit at his side’ (verse 2). The glory of God rises from above the cherubim and moves to the threshold of the temple (verse 3).

God tells the man in linen to go through the city ‘and put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Linen was the fabric of priestly clothing, and in later visions heavenly messengers also wear linen. The writing kit was a scribe's case of reed pens and ink.

The mark is the Hebrew letter tav, the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script of Ezekiel's day was written as a simple X or cross-shaped stroke. Some early Christian writers later saw a sign of the cross in it; that is a later Christian reflection. In Ezekiel the mark means that God knows his own.

Marking recalls the Passover, when blood on the doorposts marked the houses the destroyer would pass over. The glory moving to the threshold is the first step of its departure from the temple.
passages.later: At the Passover God said, ‘The blood on the houses where you are staying will distinguish them’ (Exodus 12:13).
passages.asks: The mark went on those who grieved over evil. Ask whether you grieve over wrong, or have grown used to it. And ask what it means to belong to God in a time of judgment.

passages.happening:
God tells the others to follow the man in linen through the city and strike, sparing no one except those with the mark. ‘Now begin at My sanctuary’ (verse 6). They begin with the elders before the temple, and go out through the city (verses 6-7). These notes name the killing and do not describe it.

Left alone, Ezekiel falls on his face and cries out, ‘Oh, Lord GOD, when You pour out Your wrath on Jerusalem, will You destroy the entire remnant of Israel?’ (verse 8). God answers that the iniquity of Israel and Judah is very great, and the land is full of bloodshed, because they say, ‘The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see’ (verse 9). Then the man in linen reports, ‘I have done as You commanded’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The vision is dated to 592 BC. What it portrays came in 587 or 586 BC, when the Babylonians broke through the walls, killed many of the people and burned the temple. Ezekiel presents that coming disaster as God's own judgment. In the vision the destroyers are heavenly figures; in history they would be Babylonian soldiers.

Judgment begins at the sanctuary, with the leaders who should have known better. Jeremiah records that some in Jerusalem were spared at the fall, among them Ebed-melech, who had rescued Jeremiah from a cistern. The vision puts the same truth in a picture: God tells apart those who grieve over evil from those who practice it.
passages.later: Abraham once pleaded for a city: ‘Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?’ (Genesis 18:25). Ebed-melech was spared when Jerusalem fell (Jeremiah 39:15-18).
passages.hard:
How can God command the killing of old and young, women and children, even in a vision?

This is one of the hardest passages in the prophets, and it should not be read quickly. The vision portrays the coming fall of Jerusalem, in which the Babylonian army did kill young and old alike, and it interprets that disaster as God's judgment rather than a meaningless accident. Some readers therefore take the language as a prophetic picture of real events, never a pattern for any human action. Others stress the mark: in the vision no one who grieved over the city's evil is harmed. Others note that the prophet himself cries out against it (verse 8), and that Scripture keeps his protest. None of these removes the difficulty entirely.

What the chapter does not do is present the killing as something to celebrate or imitate. It gives no one a warrant for violence. It is Israel's own Scripture, spoken to Israel's own people, and it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.
passages.asks: Ezekiel fell on his face and pleaded for his people. Ask whom you pray for when judgment seems deserved. And ask what it would mean to plead rather than condemn.
